args.text: [lane-plover] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to an old server after a move or failover, so the service looks down. (2) Slow security fixes: if a record is poisoned or hijacked, the bad answer lingers until the cache expires. (3) Delayed changes: planned switches, such as moving traffic or rotating servers, take much longer to reach everyone, and the time is hard to predict.

[lane-plover] Idempotent retries matter because a request that is repeated after a timeout or failure may already have succeeded, and an idempotent one gives the same result however many times it runs. This stops duplicate charges, orders or messages, so systems can retry safely and recover from faults without harming data.

[lane-plover] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a time-ordered unique identifier) as a primary key: (1) It leaks creation time, because the first part of the identifier is a timestamp, so outsiders can see roughly when a record was made. (2) It is larger than a plain integer key (128 bits against 64 bits), so indexes take more space and comparisons cost slightly more, though the time ordering keeps inserts far friendlier than random UUIDs.

[lane-plover] A write-ahead log is a record of every change that a database writes to durable storage before the change is applied to the main data files. If the system crashes, it replays this log to restore a consistent state, so committed work is not lost and half-finished work can be undone.

[lane-plover] (1) Pinning the client version keeps the test fair: if the client changes between runs, any difference in speed might come from the new client rather than the system being measured. (2) It makes the results repeatable, so other people can rerun the benchmark later and get comparable figures.

[lane-plover] Backpressure is a way for a queue that is filling up to signal the producers to slow down, pause or be turned away, instead of letting work pile up without limit. This protects the system from running out of memory and keeps delays predictable, because the pace of incoming work is matched to how fast it can actually be processed.

[lane-plover] A cron job can run twice when a slow run overlaps the next scheduled tick, or when the same crontab entry is deployed on several hosts or duplicated across environments. A guard is to take an exclusive lock (for example flock or a distributed lock with a lease) at the start so a second instance exits immediately, ideally combined with idempotent job logic.

[lane-plover] A tombstone is a marker written in place of a deleted record in a replicated store, so that the deletion itself can be replicated to other nodes. Without it, a replica that missed the delete could send the old value back and revive the data; tombstones are kept for a grace period and then removed by compaction.

[lane-plover] Two signs a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no changes, e.g. a rerun or retry flips the result; (2) failures depend on timing or environment, such as sleeps, ordering, shared state, or load, and they don't reproduce deterministically.

[lane-plover] A lease lock is only valid until an expiry time, and holders and the lock service each judge that expiry using their own clocks. If a holder's clock runs slow, or the server's runs fast, the holder thinks it still owns the lease after the server has expired it and granted it to someone else, so two nodes act as owner at once. Pauses (GC, VM stalls) cause the same problem, so fencing tokens and conservative expiry margins are needed.
